title: never blended as doctrine
hook: Kabir sings to Ram, but which Ram? Hindus argue it among themselves
tomorrow: one poet, one town, two tombs. which one is his?

segments.voice: Yesterday, never blended as doctrine: shared practice, separate creeds, and a grandmother who went to see a holy man and came home herself. Today, one word in Kabir's songs, argued over inside Hinduism itself.

Two cousins at a family dinner. One keeps a picture of Ram as her phone's lock screen. The other says God can't fit in any picture. The plates go quiet. Kabir sings Ram's name again and again. So which Ram? The prince of Ayodhya, with his bow, his exile and his return? A line credited to Kabir answers, in paraphrase: Dasharath's son is praised through the three worlds, but the secret of Ram's name is something else.
screen: `A LOCK SCREEN, OR NO PICTURE?` → `KABIR SINGS RAM.` → `BUT WHICH RAM?`

segments.voice: Hindu tradition has two words for this argument, and each side has a real case. Saguna means with qualities: God with a form you can picture, Ram with his bow, Krishna with his flute. Its best case is that love needs a face. A God you can see, dress, feed and sing to can be loved the way a person is loved. Tulsidas sings the Ram of Ayodhya, and his Ram has a father, a wife and a long road home. Nirguna means without qualities: God beyond form, beyond any picture. Its best case is that anything you can picture is smaller than God, and the one beyond form is found within, close as the breath. Hindu histories of bhakti place Kabir among the nirguna sants. Both are Hindu ways of loving God, and the argument goes on inside the tradition. Now the never-blended part. When Hindus took Kabir in, they didn't need Islamic doctrine to explain him. They already had a frame of their own: nirguna. A Hindu listener hears Kabir's Ram as the one within, without form. Some Muslim readers hear the same songs in their own frame: one God, beyond every image. Same line, two readings, each from its own house. Nobody had to settle what Ram finally means for the song to keep going.
screen: `SAGUNA: LOVE NEEDS A FACE.` · `NIRGUNA: BEYOND ANY PICTURE.` · `A HINDU FRAME FOR KABIR.` · then, large: `ONE NAME, TWO HOUSES.`

segments.voice: Say one sacred name out loud, softly: one that's yours, or simply the word peace. Say it a few times and notice the picture it brings. Then stop, and listen to the quiet right after it. Let both belong, the name with a face and the silence that follows.
Never blended as doctrine. Here, one name, Ram, heard with form and beyond form, each reading drawn from its own house.
For the road: never blended as doctrine, one name read from two houses. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu devotion holds both saguna bhakti, love of God with form (as in Tulsidas's Ram), and nirguna bhakti, love of God beyond form (as in Kabir's songs); devotees and teachers still discuss how the two fit together.

chat.meaning: Saguna and nirguna are both Hindu: Ram with form, as Tulsidas sings, and Ram beyond form, as Kabir sings.
